title: Jerome's Bible
hook: a grumpy genius in a Bethlehem cave translates the Bible into Latin
carry: ignorance of scripture is ignorance of christ

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambrose, the bishop who told an emperor no. Your line was no one is above it.

Gourd, or ivy? A letter carries that question from North Africa to Bethlehem. Augustine is writing to Jerome. A bishop in a town called Oea has had the book of Jonah read aloud in Jerome's new translation. At the moment God makes a plant grow up to shade the sulking prophet, the congregation hears a different plant. They know it as a gourd. Jerome's version says ivy. There's an uproar in the church, Augustine says, and the bishop nearly loses his people over one word.

Jerome was a scholar with a sharp pen and a short temper, and his letters show both. Tradition places him in Bethlehem, working near the cave where Christians remember Jesus being born. Latin-speaking Christians already had Latin Bibles, translated from the Greek by different hands, and the copies didn't agree. Jerome set out to revise them, then did something bolder. For the Old Testament, he went back past the Greek to the Hebrew. In his prefaces he calls it the Hebrew truth, and describes the hard labor of learning the language. That's how the gourd became ivy. The Hebrew word for Jonah's plant is rare, and Jerome made a choice. When Augustine wrote, worried, Jerome wrote back, not gently, and defended it. The King James translators, also working from the Hebrew, went with gourd: "And the LORD God prepared a gourd, and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shadow over his head." Readers still differ on what plant it was. Jerome's Latin went on being read and copied in the Western church long after him, and came to be called the Vulgate. And he gave a reason for the labor. In his commentary on Isaiah he writes that not to know the scriptures is not to know Christ, echoing Jesus in John's Gospel: "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me." A Bible in your own language comes through someone like Jerome, bent over a hard word, and getting letters about it.

Think of someone who has carried words across for you: whoever put the Bible, or a book you love, into your language, a parent who interpreted at the doctor, a teacher or nurse who made a hard thing clear. Picture them, and let a simple thanks rise. If you pray, thank God for them by name; if you don't, just hold the gratitude.
Vulgate. The Latin Bible tied to Jerome's work, made so people could hear scripture in the language of their own churches.
Your line: ignorance of scripture is ignorance of christ. Behind every page you read, someone chose the words. Day seven hundred seventy-eight, done.

howItsDone: Christians honor Jerome as a saint and a doctor of the church, and some remember him as a patron of translators; the Vulgate remains an official Latin text of the Catholic Church, while Christians today read the Bible in many modern translations.

chat.says: Why did Jerome bother translating from Hebrew if Latin Bibles already existed?
options: The Latin copies didn't agree, so he went back past the Greek to the Hebrew.
There were no Latin Bibles yet, so he made the very first one from scratch.
He worked only from the Greek, to keep the old wording everyone already knew.
chat.meaning: Latin Bibles existed but disagreed. Jerome revised them, and for the Old Testament went back to what he called the Hebrew truth.

notes: The Oea story: Augustine, Letter 71.3.5 (cucurbita vs hedera, a tumult in the church, the bishop nearly left without a flock). Jerome's reply: Letter 112.22. Paraphrased; confirm.
'Hebraica veritas' and the labor of learning Hebrew: from Jerome's prefaces and letters (e.g. Letter 125.12). Confirm wording 'the Hebrew truth'.
Carry source: Commentary on Isaiah, prologue ('ignoratio scripturarum ignoratio Christi est'). Paraphrased in voice; confirm.
'Tradition places him in Bethlehem, working near the cave' of the Nativity: confirm phrasing; the index says 'a Bethlehem cave'.

Not stated: that Jerome translated the whole Vulgate (scholars think parts of the New Testament beyond the Gospels are not his revision). Script says 'tied to Jerome's work'. 'Became the Bible the Western church read and copied for a very long time' is general history, not from a cited text; confirm.
No etymology of 'Vulgate' is given (claims rule). howItsDone: 'official Latin text of the Catholic Church' (Nova Vulgata) and 'patron of translators'; confirm.
